title: Listening in Mali Gaura
hook: listen to one hymn and its Bhagat verse

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mali Gaura, and your line was short and sweet. The guest at the end of it gets today.

Blessed is the wool. That's a line from the Guru Granth Sahib. Not blessed is the temple, not blessed is the king. Blessed is the wool, and the blanket made from it. It comes near the end of Mali Gaura, in the first hymn of its guest, Bhagat Namdev. So today, reading along with him slowly: why would a saint bless a sheep's coat?
screen: `BLESSED IS THE WOOL.` → `THE GUEST AT THE END.` → `READ ALONG WITH NAMDEV.`

segments.voice: Namdev's hymn starts with music. In plain English, not word for word: blessed, blessed is that flute the Lord plays; the sweet, sweet sound rings out, unstruck. That line is marked Rahao, pause, and in Sikh reading the Rahao line is the center the rest of the hymn turns around. Then Namdev starts blessing things. Blessed is the wool of the sheep. Blessed is the blanket Krishna wraps around himself. Blessed is mother Devaki, in whose home the Lord was born. Blessed is the forest of Brindaban. Namdev is singing from inside the stories of his own world, the cowherd Krishna with his flute, and Sikhs read these names as names for the one God the whole Granth praises. Watch the direction. Namdev doesn't stay with the grand things. He goes to the wool, the blanket, a mother's house, a forest. The holy, in this hymn, makes everything near it holy too: the ordinary cloth, the ordinary home. It's short enough to hear end to end in one sitting, and with the words in front of you, you can watch it walk outward from the flute to the wool. The word for sweet here is madhur, and Namdev doubles it: madhur madhur. So yesterday's line turns around. Mali Gaura was short and sweet. Namdev's verse is sweet and short.
screen: `THE FLUTE: SWEET, SWEET.` · `RAHAO: THE CENTER LINE.` · `BLESSED IS THE WOOL.` · `FROM THE FLUTE OUT TO THE BLANKET.` · then, large: `SWEET AND SHORT.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on whatever is closest, a sleeve, a cup, the chair, and notice it with care: where it came from, whose hands touched it before yours. Namdev blessed wool and a blanket; let this ordinary thing be quietly important for a minute. If you pray, say Waheguru as you look at it; if you don't, just keep your attention on it, gently.
Listening in Mali Gaura. Reading along with Bhagat Namdev's verse: the flute's sweet, sweet sound, and blessings on the wool and the blanket. Today's word.
Your line: sweet and short. In Namdev's hymn, even a blanket sits close to the holy. More tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hymns of the Bhagats, like Namdev's, are sung in kirtan in their raga just as the Gurus' hymns are, and many listeners follow the Gurmukhi text with a translation on a screen or in a book while it is sung.

chat.says: Why would a hymn in the Granth bless wool and a blanket?
options: In Namdev's hymn, the holy makes everything near it holy too, even plain cloth.
Because wool was used to wrap the Granth, so the hymn honors it.
It's a farming hymn, praying for healthy sheep and a good wool harvest.
chat.meaning: Namdev moves outward from the Lord's flute to the wool, the blanket and a mother's house. The holy makes what's near it holy too.
